_comment: Adjudicated same-molecule pairs found by pipeline/audit/structural_dupes.py — two rows sharing the full InChIKey of their largest SMILES fragment, which folds a salt onto its freebase while keeping stereochemistry so enantiomers never collapse. The detector REPORTS; only pairs recorded here are merged, because a structural collision is ambiguous: it means either a genuine duplicate or a wrong SMILES, and those have opposite fixes. That is not hypothetical: an auto-merging first version would have folded Mephenmetrazine into 4-Methylphenmetrazine, which collide only because one of the two structures is wrong — see notMerged, where that pair is still unresolved. Auto-merge destroys a real compound to 'fix' a typo, and cannot tell the two cases apart. `keep` is the survivor (the row carrying more data or the more standard forensic name); `merge` folds into it, contributing its aliases and identifiers. Applied by SQLiteBuilder.apply_structural_duplicate_merges(), which re-verifies the shared key at build time and refuses to merge a pair that no longer collides.

duplicates.why: Same cathinone; the merged row stored the hydrochloride ([Cl-]...[H+]), which yields a different full InChIKey and defeated every name-keyed merge. DEA temporary Schedule I 2018 (83 FR 44474) citing ~151 US overdose deaths, so a split row is a safety problem, not just untidiness.
Straight synonyms, and both rows already carried CAS 17763-02-9 — dedup never consulted CAS. Widespread in the current adulterated supply; keeping the name drug-checking reports actually use.
Identical SMILES; the merged row had no CAS, CID or InChIKey at all, so nothing existed to match on. Survivor holds 4 dose rows to the other's 1.
Abbreviation vs full name; the survivor is stored as the hydrochloride and the abbreviation as the freebase, which is why the InChIKeys differed.
IC-26 is Methiodone's development code. Freebase vs hydrochloride; survivor carries 3 dose rows to the other's 1.
The same compound under the two competing NBOMe naming schemes (2C-x-NBOMe vs 25x-NBOMe). Survivor has CAS, CID and 3 dose rows.
Abbreviation of the survivor's own name; the abbreviation row is stored as the hydrochloride.
Abbreviation of the survivor's own name.
MEM is the Shulgin code for this compound, and the survivor already carries 'MEM' as its display_name — so the split row was the code name duplicating its own parent.
IP is the Shulgin code for isoproscaline. The two-letter row is also an alias-collision hazard.

Same compound under two spellings of the same abbreviation. Invisible until now because 5-BR-DMT's SMILES did not sanitize at all — its indole nitrogen was written as aromatic `n` instead of `[nH]`, so the row keyed off its fumarate counterion. Corrected in identifier-corrections-manual.json, whereupon the duplicate surfaced. Independently flagged by the research-chemical auditor in the same session.

Abbreviation of the survivor's own name. The two rows carry different CAS numbers — 2338-13-8 on the survivor and 2975-41-9 on the abbreviation — which is the freebase/hydrochloride pair, not two compounds; that mismatch is exactly why no name- or identifier-keyed pass merged them. Survivor holds 5 dose rows and 23 durations to the other's 1 and 3. Flagged in the 2026-08-01 data audit's duplicate list and surfaced structurally once the alias tangle was untied.

notMerged.why: NOT a duplicate — Nabiximols (Sativex) is a botanical extract standardised to roughly 1:1 THC:CBD, so it has no single structure. Its row stores CBD's SMILES, which is why it collides. A combination product should carry no SMILES at all; left in place pending the combination-product modelling decision.

UNRESOLVED — do not merge, and do not 'correct' either structure without real evidence. Our Mephenmetrazine row stores 4-methylphenmetrazine's structure (para-methylphenyl, NH) and carries no InChIKey. A PubChem name lookup for 'mephenmetrazine' returns CID 30487 = (2S,3S)-3,4-dimethyl-2-phenylmorpholine, but that CID is PHENDIMETRAZINE, which the catalog already holds as its own marketed anorectic — so PubChem is resolving the name through a loose synonym index rather than confirming a distinct compound. Writing that structure in was tried and immediately produced a Mephenmetrazine/Phendimetrazine block-1 collision, which the PSID guard failed the build on. Needs a primary source for what 'mephenmetrazine' denotes before either row is touched.
